summary:
Earth Jukebox lets you hear when and where the Earth goes off the charts. It is a web app that turns NASA Earth data and Earth Information Center visualizations into music, based on anomaly: how far each place strays from its own historical average. Normal sounds harmonic, in D major; unusual sounds tense and dissonant.

Our main scene is Chihuahua, Mexico, region by region: night lights from the EIC (SVS 5313), lightning seen from the ISS (SVS 5011) and six climate variables from NASA POWER (2001–2024). Move your mouse, finger or arrow keys over the map and you hear the value and anomaly under the probe; step through the timeline to hear the same place change year after year. A Global lab plays planet-wide scenes, and a Collection offers 14 generated tracks to listen to like an album.

Earth data is almost entirely visual, which leaves out blind and low-vision people, and even sighted viewers miss patterns in fast animations. Earth Jukebox works with eyes closed: full keyboard control, spoken narration, a sound legend and a screen-reader panel, so anyone can find a drought or a record year by ear.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth data into sound you can explore. Every area of the map plays according to its anomaly (z-score): how unusual it is compared with its own 2001–2020 normal for that month. The app has three sections:

  • Chihuahua (main): the state of Chihuahua, Mexico, in five regions (Sierra Tarahumara, North, Central Valleys, South, Desert). It opens with the Earth Information Center night-lights visualization (SVS 5313), showing each year's frame, and covers temperature, maximum heat, rain, soil moisture, wind, sunlight and ISS lightning.
  • Global lab: planet-wide scenes decoded from Scientific Visualization Studio videos: night lights, lightning and aerosols.
  • Collection: 14 pre-rendered tracks with explanations, for listening without interacting.

HOW TO USE IT

Explore with the mouse, a finger or the keyboard: arrows move the probe, Page Up/Down change the date, A jumps to the most unusual area, Space replays the sound and L plays the sound legend. Click any of Chihuahua's 67 municipalities, or press Enter on it, and a natural voice reads its card: its people and a curious fact from the NASA data. The "What you hear" panel says the region, the value, the anomaly in standard deviations, the difference in real units (e.g. "−1.6 mm/day vs the September normal") and which chord is playing, and screen readers read it aloud. A Legend button plays what normal, below-normal and above-normal sound like, and optional narration announces the date and the most unusual region.

THE SOUND GRAMMAR (the same in every scene)

- A cello drone in D is "normal": a fixed reference, like the grid lines of a chart.

- The chord shows how unusual it is: D major = normal; going below adds sus2 → minor → low cluster; going above adds maj9 → lydian → high cluster.

- Each variable has its own voice, chosen for how the phenomenon feels: rain is a falling piano line (more rain = faster, louder, higher), heat is an oboe, wind a flute, lightning timpani thunder, night lights a Rhodes. Zero means silence.

- Stereo pan = longitude (west left, east right); the room reverb follows the land cover under the probe (read from MODIS via NASA GIBS); a bell marks a record.

- Everything stays in one key, so the data move a few dials inside a song instead of producing noise.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Heavy processing happens offline and is published as static files. A Node script downloads monthly NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 and CERES) for the state. A Python pipeline decodes SVS/EIC videos pixel by pixel into data grids (brightness for night lights, yellow-pixel area for lightning, legend colors for aerosols). In the browser, the app computes each cell's normal, standard deviation and z-score, samples the exact value under the probe, and synthesizes the music live. NASA GIBS tiles provide the base map, the layer for each month and the land cover under the probe.

Tools: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Zustand, MapLibre GL, Tone.js with real instrument samples, Python, Node.js, the Web Speech API and Kokoro, an open neural text-to-speech model, for the municipality voices. A desktop version for Windows (WinUI 3 + C++) renders the Collection.

VALIDATION

We compared our Chihuahua file with the NASA POWER point API over all 288 months: identical values for rain and temperature. Known events show up where they should: the 2011 and 2023–2024 droughts are the driest years, and 2023–2024 the hottest. We measured the night-lights georeferencing against 12 cities and corrected a 0.375° offset. An automated test checks the musical score of all 27 scenes against the real data.

WHY IT MATTERS AND WHAT IS CREATIVE

Hearing is excellent at noticing what breaks a pattern. Using the standard climate-science anomaly method keeps the sound scientifically meaningful, not decorative, and the fixed grammar means that once you learn one scene you can listen to all of them. We designed for blind and low-vision users from the start rather than adding accessibility at the end.

LIMITATIONS WE CONSIDERED

Climate variables come from MERRA-2 reanalysis (about 55 km cells), not weather stations, and are least certain for rain in mountains. Night lights are relative brightness (0–1) because the SVS color bar has no units. Lightning depends on when the ISS passes over. These limits are explained inside the app ("How it works").

IMPACT

Earth Jukebox could be used at the Earth Information Center, in classrooms and in museums, letting anyone, sighted or not, investigate Earth data by ear.
